messages.subject: Quadrupled Predict Values
parts:
All,

First off, I have only been working with unmarked for a few weeks now. Top-notch work from all contributors. I am excited to see where the models go.

Model selection: pcountOpen()

Data for detection matrix (y): I have 21 routes that have been sampled twice a year for 5 years. Each route consists of multiple stations in which an observer listens for the study organism. Multiple individuals can be recorded at each station, so the data are not binary. The detection matrix is 21 rows by 10 columns. The data are sums of detections from each site on a route for that year and replicate.

Example Mock Data:
y <- matrix(sample(0:12, 21*10, replace=TRUE), nrow=21, ncol=10)
y <- data.frame(y)
names(y) <- c("2020.1", "2020.2", "2021.1", "2021.2", "2022.1", "2022.2", "2023.1", "2023.2", "2024.1", "2024.2")
routes <- LETTERS[1:21]
row.names(y) <- routes

Data for yearlyCovs: I am using Year here since I would like to see how the population is changing over the 5 year period. This data.frame is has 21 rows and 5 columns (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024). I have coded this data to with help from this example . This data is 21 rows x 5 columns.

Example Data:
years.df <- data.frame(Routes=routes,
                    year.2020=rep("yr1", times=21),
                    year.2021=rep("yr2", times=21),
                    year.2022=rep("yr3", times=21),
                    year.2023=rep("yr4", times=21),
                    year.2024=rep("yr5", times=21))
years.df <- as.data.frame(apply(years.df, 2, as.factor))
row.names(years.df) <- routes
yearlyCovs <- list(Years=years.df[,-1])


Data for obsCovs: I am using Sunrise.Diff, which is the difference from observed time at a station and sunrise for that station on that specific day. By using the reshape package, I was able to find the mean value sunrise.diff along the route during the visit. This matrix is 21 rows x 10 columns.

Example Mock Data:

sunrise <- matrix(rnorm(21*10, mean=0, sd=1), nrow=21, ncol=10)
sunrise.df <- data.frame(sunrise)
names(sunrise.df) <- c("2020.1", "2020.2", "2021.1", "2021.2", "2022.1", "2022.2", "2023.1", "2023.2", "2024.1", "2024.2")
row.names(sunrise.df) <- routes
obsCovs <- list(Sunrise.Diff=as.matrix(sunrise.df))

I feed these into 
umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y=y, obsCov=obsCovs, yearlySiteCovs=yearlyCovs, numPrimary=5)

Then run the model
m1 <- pcountOpen(lambdaformula=~1, gammaformula=~1, omegaformula=~Years, pformula=~Sunrise.Diff, data=umf)


The summary of the actual (not from mock data) model is below:

Call:
pcountOpen(lambdaformula = ~1, gammaformula = ~1, omegaformula = ~Years,
    pformula = ~Sunrise.Diff, data = umf)

Abundance (log-scale):
 Estimate    SE  z  P(>|z|)
     1.86 0.169 11 2.66e-28

Recruitment (log-scale):
 Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)
   -0.624 0.533 -1.17   0.242

Apparent Survival (logit-scale):
            Estimate     SE       z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    0.930  0.476  1.9529  0.0508
Yearsyr2      -0.162  0.774 -0.2091  0.8344
Yearsyr3       0.107  0.737  0.1453  0.8845
Yearsyr4       7.787 92.204  0.0845  0.9327

Detection (logit-scale):
             Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -0.518 0.220 -2.36  0.0184
Sunrise.Diff    0.558 0.232  2.41  0.0161

AIC: 725.6491
Number of sites: 21

Warning message:
Large or missing SE values. Be very cautious using these results.




BUT, the issue comes when I use:
m1abund.predict <- predict(m1, "omega", appendData=TRUE)

This is giving me 84 rows, rather than 21. The data is quadrupled.


Questions:
  1. Am I applying the correct model (pcountOpen) for my data?
  2. Have I coded my covariates correctly for the model?
  3. Is the large SE coming from a data problem or a labeling problem?
  4. It seems I am seeing a significant p-value with Sunrise.Diff and abundance; however, the large SE for "Yearsyr4" is worrisome. Would this value indicate the entire model cannot be interpreted or just the years portion from survival?
  5. Is the 84 rows from the predict function a data issue or coding issue?


It really seems like I have not set something up properly, but I just can't figure it out. Any help is greatly appreciated.

If the actual data are needed, I can respond to this thread with an .RData file containing the objects I am attempting to fit to the model.

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Quadrupled Predict Values
parts:
1. The open-population N-mixture model (pcountOpen) does seem compatible with your data, assuming things like population closure between the two replicates within each year. I think 21 sites is a pretty small sample size for this model, which is data hungry. If you are mostly interested in estimating a population trend over time, a stacked single-season N-mixture model might work better (search the listserv for previous discussion on this).

2. The year covariate looks correct to me.

3/4. There's definitely a problem with yr4 that I would want to solve before using this model. Maybe you have very few detections in year 4? I'd look at the data for year 4 and compare to the other years to try to figure out what's different.

5. When you call predict(..., "omega"), you are predicting values for survival. You have 5 years, which means there are 4 survival "periods" (1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5). Predict returns an estimate of survival for each site and period, 21*4 = 84 rows.

Ken

Ken (et al.),

I have been pouring over these inflated SE and Estimates for awhile now and I might have an idea, but I thought I would run in by the group.

Initially, I was treating Years as a factor (Year1, Year2, Year3, Year4, and Year5). Would this result in a categorical analysis of the survival and recruitment rather than a continuous treatment? I recoded the years as numeric (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) and I do not get the inflated SE or Estimate values. But, by doing this, I am not able to see year2 -> year3 survival. It would be an overall survival (over a time period of 5 years), correct?  I am much more interested in trends overtime, rather than how specific years compare, so this seems logically correct. 

Any input is greatly appreciated.
